item.title: Cellular and mitochondrial correlates of regional glucose metabolism in the human cortex
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Regional differences in human brain glucose metabolism reflect local energy demands, but their cellular and mitochondrial determinants remain unclear. We combined [18F]FDG positron emission tomography in healthy human participants with estimates of cellular composition and mitochondrial density to unravel (sub)cellular correlates of heterogeneity in brain glucose metabolism. By correcting for RNA content and differential gene expression due to postmortem sampling, we addressed methodological shortcomings in multimodal neuroimaging integration. We introduce transcriptionally derived cytoarchitectonic maps of the human cortex that are consistent with histological findings, providing a biologically grounded framework for relating in vivo neuroimaging signals. Accordingly, mitochondrial distribution showed strong association with the intrinsic energy requirements at resting state. In contrast, relations between metabolism and neuronal composition were driven by sensory input and mitochondria-sparse thin-axon neurons, suggesting that stimulation-induced energy demand is met rather by neuronal processes that are independent of mitochondrial abundance to maintain efficient information processing.

item.title: Resting state fMRI detects pathological functional brain connectivity in the Ndufs4 knockout mouse model of Leigh syndrome during the pre-symptomatic stage of the disease
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Leigh syndrome (LS) is a progressive encephalopathy and generally regarded as the most common inborn mitochondrial disease. Mutations in mitochondrial respiratory complex I are common in patients with LS and a mutational hotspot has been identified in the gene that encodes the NDUFS4 subunit of respiratory complex I. The Ndufs4 knockout mouse (Ndufs4 KO) model of LS closely resembles the phenotypes of LS patients and show like the patient brain lesions when the symptoms are manifested. It is speculated but unproven that brain functional connectivity may precede the onset of symptoms. Therefore, the present study was set out to investigate the progression of brain functional connectives in Ndufs4 KO mice before and after the manifestation of LS-like symptoms using in vivo resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (rs-fMRI). Since the brain lesions may be caused by increased reactive oxygen species (ROS) in the brain, we also examined the potential protective effect of KH176, a small molecular for modulating ROS levels, on brain functional connectivity. Rs-fMRI results showed that in Ndufs4 KO mice the functional connectivity of the piriform cortex, motor cortex, barrel cortex, visual cortex, auditory cortex, prefrontal cortex, lateral striatum, ventral striatum cortex and amygdala was increased, starting from the pre-symptomatic stage (middle stage) to the symptomatic stage (late stage) of the disease. KH176 had no effect on the changes in functional connectivity in the mice. In conclusion, these results show that there are abnormalities in functional connectivity in Ndufs4 KO mice during the pre-symptomatic phase of the disease and that KH176 treatment does not modify the connectivity changes.

item.title: Age and sex impact resting-state EEG aperiodic activity beyond symptom associations in persistent post-concussive symptoms
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Objective: to investigate whether resting-state EEG aperiodic parameters (i.e., offset and exponent) are associated with symptom burden and demographic factors in patients with persistent post-concussive symptoms (PPCS) and differ from healthy controls. Methods: In this cross-sectional observational study, resting-state eye-closed high-density EEG was recorded in patients with PPCS and in age-matched healthy controls. Aperiodic parameters were extracted from EEG power spectra. In patients, hierarchical multiple linear regression models included age and sex as a base model, with additional demographic and clinical symptoms entered separately. Patient-control differences were assessed using multiple linear regression adjusted for age and sex. Results: Seventy patients with PPCS (54 female; 39.57 ±12.21 y.; 109.5 [76.5; 196] days post-concussion) recruited from a concussion care pathway and 38 healthy controls (17 female; 39.61± 13.57 y.) were included. In patients, younger age and male sex were associated with higher offset and exponent values (all p under .014). None of the additional demographic and clinical variables improved model fit beyond age and sex (all p under.143). After adjustment for age and sex, neither offset (p=.898) nor exponent (p=.100) differed between patients and controls. Conclusion: Resting-state aperiodic EEG parameters were consistently associated with age and sex, but not with self-reported symptom burden or clinical characteristics in patients with PPCS. Not accounting for these factors may generate apparent group differences attributable, at least in part, to demographic variability. Significance: Age and sex are important sources of inter-individual variability in resting-state aperiodic EEG activity and should be systematically considered when investigating such features.

item.title: Post-Learning Reactivation of Memories for Naturalistic Continuous Experiences
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Memories are not static records of the past; rather, the act of remembering can change how an event is recalled. Intriguingly, several studies also suggest that memories may be reactivated during rest. However, reactivation has largely been studied for spatial tasks and discrete stimuli, and we know little about whether spontaneous reactivation occurs for long timescale naturalistic events and how reactivation affects retention. Using fMRI, we show that neural activity patterns in the hippocampus and the Default Mode Network during encoding of narrative events were spontaneously reactivated during rest. Contrary to predictions, reactivation did not strengthen recall of movie details, and instead exploratory analyses suggested that reactivation in the hippocampus was associated with more gist-like recall one week later. These findings support the idea that memories for complex events may be spontaneously reactivated, but they suggest that rather than simply strengthening episodic memories, reactivation might help transform them.

item.title: Longitudinal fMRI reveals altered developmental trajectories of functional network organisation associated with adolescent cannabis use
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Adolescence is a critical period of brain development during which the endocannabinoid system continues to mature. These developmental changes may contribute to age-related differences in the association between cannabis use and large-scale functional network organisation, yet this association remains incompletely characterised. We hypothesised that regular cannabis use would be associated with differential one-year changes in resting-state functional connectivity between adolescents and adults. Resting-state fMRI data at two time points, one year apart, were analysed from 66 participants (31 aged 16-17 years; 35 aged 26-29 years) including 29 with regular cannabis use and 37 age-matched cannabis-naive controls. Seed-to-voxel analyses examined longitudinal changes in functional connectivity across age and cannabis-use groups. Year change, age by user-group interactions were identified in salience and default mode network connectivity, including divergent changes in anticorrelations with medial prefrontal, thalamic, cerebellar and juxtapositional regions. Directionality of effects differed by network and region. Additional main effects of user group were observed for executive control and associative striatal connectivity, with the cannabis-use group showing decreased positive connectivity and reduced anticorrelation, respectively. Changes in functional connectivity were developmentally dissociable and predominantly observed in regions contributing to attentional and transmodal processing. These findings suggest that cannabis may be associated with alterations in the maturational refinement of higher-order neural systems, potentially reflecting age-related differences in neurobiological sensitivity to cannabis exposure. Considering developmental stage may therefore be important for characterising cannabis-related neurobiological differences and may have implications for understanding age-dependent vulnerability to cannabis-related psychiatric outcomes.

item.title: Predicting alcohol consumption from resting-state functional connectivity: Feature relevance and the potential of meta-matching.
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Alcohol use disorder (AUD) is among the most prevalent mental disorders. Associations between resting-state fMRI functional connectivity (FC) and AUD have been reported but rarely replicated. In this preregistered study, we investigated the extent to which FC predicts alcohol consumption, as measured by the AUDIT-C score, in a large sample of non-treatment-seeking alcohol consumers (N = 739), including 528 participants with varying degrees of AUD severity. To optimize performance, we compared kernel ridge regression (KRR) trained directly on this sample with transfer-learning models based on multilayer meta-matching embeddings, from which we derived data-driven relevance maps at the connection, region, and network levels. We tested split-half reliability, reproducibility across cohorts, and outcome specificity of the relevance maps. Both models predicted AUDIT-C scores moderately but significantly (r ≈ 0.15). Meta-matching did not outperform KRR in prediction. Relevance maps showed limited split-half reliability, consistent with the modest predictive performance, but reproduced moderately well across two independent cohorts. These maps indicate reduced connectivity among limbic regions, the anterior middle temporal gyrus, the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex, and dorsal attention network regions. In contrast, hypothesized hyperconnectivity patterns involving the striatum, anterior cingulate cortex, and precuneus were less reliable and mostly non-significant. Overall, our findings suggest that resting-state FC contains reproducible but weak signals related to alcohol consumption. Transfer learning improved relevance-map reliability but not prediction performance and reduced outcome specificity. These results support the utility of interpretable machine learning for identifying connectivity patterns related to drinking behavior, while also highlighting current limitations in its predictive power.

item.title: Altered intersubject variability of functional connectivity in gray and white matter underlying neurocognition and genetic profiles in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.
item.description:
Neural regeneration research
Abstract Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder is an autoimmune disease that causes inflammatory damage to the central nervous system. While alterations in functional connectivity have been reported in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, changes in intersubject variability of functional connectivity within gray matter and white matter are not yet understood. A total of 66 patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and 71 healthy controls were recruited. We compared intersubject variability of functional connectivity between patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and healthy controls and performed subgroup analyses comparing neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder patients with and without a history of optic neuritis. We also examined the associations between intersubject variability of functional connectivity alterations and disease duration, clinical disability, and cognitive scores. We combined our imaging results with those of the Allen Human Brain Atlas to conduct transcriptome-neuroimaging association analyses, identified gene expression profiles linked to intersubject variability of functional connectivity alterations and characterized their potential biological functions. Compared with healthy controls, patients with neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder showed widespread increases in intersubject variability of functional connectivity. Notable gray matter alterations included the precentral and postcentral gyri; extensive occipital areas; and the insula, putamen, and thalamus. The corresponding white matter changes involved the fornix, corticospinal tract, widespread corona radiata, cingulum, and uncinate fasciculus. Compared with patients without optic neuritis, the optic neuritis subgroup exhibited distinct intersubject variability of functional connectivity alterations in specific regions, such as the inferior parietal lobule, angular gyrus, thalamus, fornix, and internal capsule. Clinically, only white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity correlated significantly with physical disability and cognitive processing speed and was not significantly associated with disease duration. Transcriptomic analysis revealed that genes positively associated with white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity were enriched in synaptic plasticity and cognition, while negatively associated genes were enriched in oxidative stress. Additionally, genes positively associated with the gray matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity were enriched in myelination and lipid biosynthesis, whereas genes negatively associated with the gray matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity were involved in synapse organization. In conclusion, our study revealed alterations in gray matter- and white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity across neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder and clinical subtypes. We demonstrate that changes in white matter-intersubject variability of functional connectivity correlate with clinical disability and neurocognition. Linking these connectivity patterns with gene expression profiles may provide insights into the underlying pathophysiology of neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.

item.title: Slow Ionic Dynamics Reshape Bistability in a Biophysical Mean-Field Model of Brain Activity
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Brain states such as sleep, seizures, and resting wakefulness are often described in terms of transitions between distinct population states. Biophysically inspired mean-field models that couple neuronal firing statistics to slow ionic homeostasis provide a mechanistic bridge between detailed single-neuron physiology and macroscopic brain activity. Here we examine this issue in a biophysical mean-field model of cortical populations driven by potassium exchange and compare its dynamical repertoire with a matched spiking network across six physiological and pathological regimes. The fast subsystem contains a substantial region in which low- and high-activity fixed points coexist, but this conditional bistability is not inherited by the physiological resting branch of the complete slow-fast system. A generic fast-slow calculation identifies how feedback through a dynamical ionic variable changes the stability conditions of the fast subsystem, and an exact equilibrium reduction of the KIonEx-MF equations yields a single equilibrium on the physiological resting branch over the range examined. This resting state is excitable: perturbations generate intermittent synchronized events in both the mean-field and spiking-network descriptions. The results show how slow ionic dynamics can reshape conclusions drawn from a frozen fast subsystem and provide noise-driven excitability as an alternative route to spontaneous population transitions.

item.title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. Methods: We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. Results: ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). Discussion: These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

item.title: EEG Biomarkers for Rett Syndrome: A Comparative Analysis of Machine Learning and Deep Learning with Explainable AI
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder characterised by abnormal cortical activity, which can be captured using electroencephalography (EEG). Although machine learning (ML) has shown promise for diagnosing several neurological conditions, comprehensive evaluation of classical ML and deep learning (DL) methods, together with physiologically meaningful explanations, remains limited for RTT. This study analyses resting-state, eyes-closed EEG recordings from RTT patients and healthy controls using both power spectral density (PSD)-based ML and end-to-end DL frameworks. Classical ML models, including Support Vector Machines, Random Forest, and XGBoost, were trained on PSD features, while EEG-specific DL architectures, including ShallowConvNet, DeepConvNet, EEGNet, and EEG Conformer, were trained directly on preprocessed EEG signals. Subject-wise cross-validation was used to avoid data leakage, with balanced accuracy as the primary performance metric because it equally accounts for sensitivity and specificity. Random Forest achieved the best performance among the classical ML models, whereas EEGNet achieved the highest DL performance. An ablation study indicated that 4-second EEG epochs offered the optimal trade-off between model performance and robustness. Model interpretability was investigated using SHAP for Random Forest and occlusion sensitivity analysis for EEGNet. Both methods consistently identified delta and theta oscillations, along with centro-frontal brain regions, as key contributors to RTT classification. These findings show that both PSD-based machine learning and end-to-end deep learning methods can reliably identify RTT and highlight common neurophysiological biomarkers, offering an interpretable framework for EEG-based diagnosis and biomarker discovery for Rett Syndrome.

item.title: The SPOT Grid: Naturalistic images with predefined settings, patterns, objects, and textures.
item.description:
Behavior research methods
In the natural world, higher-level visual features (e.g., scenes and objects) systematically covary with specific lower-level constituent features (e.g., textures and patterns). This natural covariation makes it difficult to isolate aspects of behavior or brain activity that are specific to a single level of the feature hierarchy. For example, a particular neural or behavioral response may reflect recognition of a "jungle" scene, or it may reflect sensitivity to the lower-level features - leaf textures, dense vertical lines, etc. - that constitute jungle scenes. To address this challenge, we developed a novel approach for partially decoupling higher- and lower-level features in naturalistic images. We employed a Stable Diffusion image generation framework to create a naturalistic image set in which setting-object pairings and texture-pattern pairings are factorially combined, enabling systematic manipulation of higher-level and lower-level image content. To validate our approach, we used state-of-the-art image-processing models to confirm that higher-level features are represented similarly regardless of their lower-level constituents and, conversely, that lower-level features are represented similarly regardless of the higher-level objects/settings they constitute. We then confirmed that human participants can readily and rapidly categorize these features in our generated images. We present the image generation framework and introduce the SPOT (Settings, Patterns, Objects, Textures) Grid, a publicly available stimulus set accompanied by image-specific metrics (upon request: forms.gle/X2HpzRYUGigFS1S27). This resource provides new opportunities for investigating hierarchical visual representations, feature binding, and abstraction across perception, behavior, and the brain.

item.title: Human similarity judgments reveal fine-grained representations of dynamic social scenes
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
How does the human mind organize dynamic social scenes? Existing accounts rely on pre-defined social-affective or action-based taxonomies, yet whether humans use these dimensions to structure their representations of naturalistic social scenes remains unknown. We collected 53,223 human similarity judgments of videos depicting two-person actions and trained a sparse-positive-embedding model to recover the underlying latent dimensions. These learned dimensions explained twice as much variance in similarity judgments as pre-labeled annotations, captured interpretable fine-grained social-event structure (combining information about social relationships and actions), and fractionated broad semantic content (e.g., separating parent-child interactions into caregiving versus affectionate play). The same dimensions also predicted fMRI responses to passively viewed stimuli across visual cortex better than pre-labeled annotations, highlighting their importance beyond similarity judgments. Together, these results suggest that humans represent dynamic social scenes along fine-grained axes not captured by current taxonomies, and offer behaviorally-grounded targets for future studies of social vision.

item.title: Correction-stage information leakage and target-input asymmetry can distort comparisons of fNIRS short-separation channel correction strategies.
item.description:
Physiological measurement
Objective We examined how evaluation design affects comparisons of functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) short-separation correction strategies. Approach Nearest-SC, All-SC, SC-PCA and an adapted tCCA-GLM were compared in a multimodal resting-state dataset (n = 14), using semi-nested and correction-stage fully nested cross-validation, boundary purging, symmetric leave-one-modality-out (LOMO) evaluation, circular-shift nulls, injected hemodynamic response function (HRF) recovery and a second cohort. Main results In an initial joint-target diagnostic analysis, the adapted tCCA-GLM's absolute out-of-fold R² increased by 42.7 percentage points from semi-nested to purged fully nested evaluation. In a separate fixed-seed purged analysis, its null-adjusted ΔR² was -1.1%. Symmetric LOMO, which evaluates reduced tCCA models, yielded no statistically detected method differences (all paired p ≥ 0.3685), but did not establish equivalence or separately quantify leakage and input-target overlap. Motion-targeted external validation provided partial support for an evaluation-tier × method interaction (Freedman-Lane p < 0.005). SC-PCA had lower mean known-truth normalized root mean square error (nRMSE = 0.037) than the adapted tCCA-GLM (0.121); within-metric Holm-adjusted comparisons were significant for this contrast and for amplitude-bias comparisons with all three SC-based strategies, but not for slopes. Sensitivity analyses included training-fold PCA selection, LOMO boundary/segment-filtering checks, lagged evaluation and longer test blocks. Significance Benchmarks should fit learned correction stages within training data, disclose correction-evaluation overlap and assess signal preservation separately. Findings are specific to the evaluated implementations, outcomes and datasets; the sensitivity analyses do not establish complete removal of preprocessing-related dependence.

item.title: Action features dominate cortical representation during natural vision.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Cortical resources are allocated into systems specialized for processing ecologically relevant features of the world. These features are typically studied in isolation using controlled experimental stimuli, making it difficult to assess the relative importance of different kinds of features that tend to overlap during natural vision. In the current study, we evaluated the relative contributions of action, agent, and scene features in predicting cortical activity while participants viewed a 1-h nature documentary. We tested four sets of model features: semantic vectors capturing the observed action, agent, and scene features derived from an annotation of the stimulus, as well as low-level visual motion-energy features. We used banded ridge regression to fit vertex-wise encoding models from the combination of all four sets of features. While each set of features predicted neural activity in the expected areas, the action features predicted more widespread activity. A variance partitioning analysis revealed that the action features captured the most unique variance in neural activity across a much larger extent of cortex than the agent or scene features. Our findings suggest that cortical activity during dynamic, natural vision is dominated by features for understanding the actions of others.

item.title: Multimodal associations between posterior hippocampus glutamate metabolism, visual cortex connectivity, and intrusive trauma reexperiencing symptoms.
item.description:
Molecular psychiatry
Hippocampal dysfunction is implicated in posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), particularly intrusive reexperiencing symptoms, and may be mediated by glutamatergic excitotoxicity. Markers of glutamate dysfunction (higher glutamate to N-acetyl aspartate levels; Glu/NAA) in the hippocampus (HPC) have been linked to reexperiencing symptoms. However, the HPC demonstrates heterogeneity along its anterior-posterior axis, with different functional connectivity patterns and PTSD symptom associations, motivating investigations into glutamate metabolism in anterior and posterior HPC subregions (a/pHPC). To this end, 121 symptomatic trauma-exposed adults with current trauma reexperiencing symptoms completed magnetic resonance spectroscopy and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging to examine the regional specificity of HPC Glu/NAA associations with reexperiencing symptoms and the link to a/pHPC functional connectivity. PTSD symptoms were assessed with the Clinician-Administered PTSD Scale for DSM-5. Reexperiencing symptom severity was associated with greater Glu/NAA in the pHPC, but not aHPC. pHPC Glu/NAA was further linked to stronger functional connectivity between the pHPC and visual cortex (VC), which in turn correlated with more severe reexperiencing symptoms. This strengthened pHPC-VC connectivity explained the shared variance between pHPC Glu/NAA and reexperiencing severity, suggesting dysregulated glutamate metabolism in the pHPC may contribute to reexperiencing symptoms through functional connectivity with the VC. These findings replicate prior work linking HPC Glu/NAA to trauma reexperiencing symptoms and provide novel evidence of this association in the pHPC, but not aHPC, which is mediated by its functional connectivity with the VC. This multimodal investigation supports translational models of glutamatergic dysfunction in trauma-related disorders and highlights new targets for pharmacological and neuromodulatory interventions.

item.title: Decoding individual differences in mental information from human brain responses predicted by deep neural networks.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Brain decoding using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) has high potential for evaluating unobservable mental information that varies across individuals in everyday situations. Although estimating individual differences in mental information using brain decoding could be effective for social applications, especially in neuromarketing, the physical constraints and high costs of fMRI limit the practical application in real-world settings. To overcome these limitations, we propose a framework to estimate individual differences in decodable mental information using brain responses predicted by deep neural networks (DNNs). In this framework, DNN-based models are trained to predict fMRI responses to natural movie scenes. Then, additional fMRI measurements are no longer required because mental information for new movie scenes can be decoded from the predicted responses instead of the measured ones. A large-scale analysis revealed that the proposed predicted-response decoding captures individual difference patterns consistent with those derived from conventional measured-response decoding across various cognitive domains. Of the 88 cognitive labels associated with movie scenes, individual difference patterns could be captured for more than 70% of the labels. This framework offers a promising approach for evaluating personal mental information with substantially reduced reliance on fMRI, thereby expanding the potential for social applications of brain decoding.

item.title: Translational evidence for habenula's role in human addiction: A scoping review.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Addiction is characterized by persistent substance use or engagement in behaviors despite adverse consequences and impaired control, but its expression varies substantially across individuals, substances, and severity. Within one influential neurocircuitry framework, addiction processes are organized into binge, withdrawal, and preoccupation stages. Preclinical research implicates the habenula across these processes but indicates that its contribution varies across drugs, subdivisions, and experimental models. Research on the human habenula in addiction remains fragmented, and the extent to which it converges with preclinical mechanisms is unclear. This scoping review synthesized evidence on the human habenula in addiction and examined its convergence with preclinical findings. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, databases and grey literature were searched in November 2025, with literature surveillance continued through April 2026. Human studies reported reduced fronto-habenula white-matter integrity, elevated habenula-striatal resting-state functional connectivity, withdrawal-related habenula-frontal connectivity, increased habenula blood flow during opioid withdrawal, altered task-evoked responses to reward and feedback, and nicotine-related genetic signals. By contrast, morphological studies found no consistent differences in habenula structure across addiction samples. Most human neuroimaging studies could not distinguish the medial and lateral habenula, limiting direct comparison with subdivision-specific preclinical mechanisms. Overall, across human and preclinical studies, the evidence does not support a unitary habenular alteration across addiction. Cross-species convergence was strongest for withdrawal-related activity, particularly for opioids, and for nicotine-related molecular mechanisms, but remained limited by differences in substances, circuits, measures, and paradigms. Future studies using subdivision-sensitive imaging and more comparable cross-species designs are needed.

item.title: Insular subregional dysfunction in panic disorder: A multimodal MRI study.
item.description:
Journal of affective disorders
Background The spatial organization of insular abnormalities across connectional-architecture-defined subregions in panic disorder (PD) remains unclear. We examined structural and resting-state functional measures using the Brainnetome Atlas. Methods Forty-nine medication-naïve patients with PD and Fifty healthy controls underwent structural and resting-state MRI. Gray matter volume (GMV), amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF), and regional homogeneity (ReHo) were assessed across six insular subregions. Four prespecified functional connections were examined, together with exploratory Granger causality analysis between dIg and S1 and an AAL3 whole-insula comparison. Results dIg-S1 functional connectivity was reduced in PD (β = -0.148, 95% CI [-0.248, -0.048], pFDR = 0.017). ALFF showed a Group × Subregion interaction (F(5,578) = 4.162, p = 0.001). Only the ventral agranular insula (vIa) showed significantly higher ALFF after false discovery rate (FDR) correction (pFDR = 0.016), with a larger group effect than other subregions. The interaction persisted after temporal signal-to-noise ratio (tSNR) adjustment (F(5,577) = 2.582, p = 0.025), but the vIa-specific effect was nonsignificant in a separate vIa-only tSNR-adjusted model (p = 0.194). ReHo was directionally lower across all six subregions, but no contrast survived FDR correction. No robust subregional GMV differences or significant group differences in exploratory Granger causality were detected. Adjusted AAL3 whole-insula differences were nonsignificant. Conclusions PD showed measure-dependent insular functional alterations, including reduced dIg-S1 coupling and vIa-predominant ALFF differences, with the latter sensitive to signal quality and spatial smoothing.

item.title: Infant Negative Affect During Mother-Infant Interaction Is Associated with Neonatal Limbic-Prefrontal Connectivity in the First Month of Life.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry. Cognitive neuroscience and neuroimaging
Background Early caregiving may shape neonatal limbic circuit organization, yet whether microanalytically coded interaction quality relates to neonatal limbic-prefrontal connectivity is unknown. We tested associations between infant and maternal affect during mother-infant interaction and neonatal limbic-prefrontal cortex (PFC) connectivity. Methods At approximately 30 days postnatal, 143 mother-infant dyads from the Healthy MiNDS cohort (São Paulo, Brazil) completed a video-recorded interaction coded with the Coding Interactive Behavior (CIB) system; infant negative affect was the percentage of interaction time in distress. Neonates underwent resting-state fMRI; limbic-PFC connectivity was quantified by principal component analysis of amygdala and hippocampus seed-to-ROI maps. Covariate-adjusted regressions tested associations. Results Infant negative affect was associated with right amygdala-PFC (β = -0.247, p = .003) and right hippocampus-PFC connectivity (β = -0.202, p = .021), both surviving FDR correction and robust across multiple analytic approaches. The amygdala association was limited to infant distress-related behaviors, whereas maternal positive expressiveness showed an independent, opposing association (β = 0.202, p = .019); no other CIB measure was significant. Exploratorily, connectivity was associated with sleep problems at 18-24 months in females (r = -.324, p = .030). Conclusions The emotional quality of early caregiving is associated with neonatal limbic circuit organization: infant distress is selectively associated with weaker amygdala-PFC connectivity, whereas maternal positive affect shows an independent opposing association. These findings identify the mother-infant relationship as a modifiable input to neonatal brain development.

item.title: The Spectrum within the Spectrum: Neural Heterogeneity in Autism.
item.description:
Behavioural brain research
Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) encompasses diverse behavioral, cognitive, and neural profiles that vary widely across individuals. Because diagnosis remains predominantly behavior-based, clinically meaningful within-spectrum differences are often missed. Recent advances in neuroimaging analysis have created opportunities for the identification of distinct neural profiles within ASD. These new avenues provide ways to examine intra-ASD heterogeneity directly, identifying person-specific brain-behavior patterns that group-level comparisons fail to capture. The present systematic review focused on neuroimaging methods (i.e., resting-state fMRI; rs-fMRI, cortical morphology) that emphasized heterogeneity-informed outcomes based on normative modeling, data-driven subtyping, clustering analysis and similar analytic choices. For rs-fMRI, findings showed that differences in connectivity within the default mode and salience networks were linked to social-communication and language impairments, with subtype-specific patterns emerging across samples. In cortical thickness and surface area, studies identified distinct developmental trajectories and individual deviation profiles, with prefrontal and temporal regions often tied to repetitive behaviors and social-communication difficulties. Voxel-based analyses revealed subgroup-specific gray matter alterations, including cerebellar and cortical differences, that aligned with variation in repetitive behaviors and social difficulties. Collectively, this emerging evidence supports the notion that neural heterogeneity in autism is a core feature rather than a limitation. Embracing individual variability can provide crucial insight into the inconsistencies and contradictions of earlier case-control and group-level findings. Moving forward, autism research must prioritize heterogeneity-based methods to establish reproducible subtypes and individualized brain-behavior links.

item.title: Movement-specific effects of transcranial magnetic stimulation over premotor and parietal cortices after stroke
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) has been proposed to support post-stroke motor recovery, but the response may depend on the task and motor-network status. We aimed to compare how premotor and parietal stimulation affects performance across reach directions with different movement demands, in preparation for therapeutic application of TMS. Methods: 16 participants with chronic subcortical stroke performed planar reaches with the KINARM exoskeleton toward distal and proximal targets. Before movement, a 10-Hz triple-pulse TMS train was delivered over bilateral dorsal or ventral premotor cortex (PMd, PMv) or dorsomedial posterior parietal cortex (PPC) at subthreshold and suprathreshold intensities. The parietal midline was used as the control target. Participant-level bootstrap confidence intervals assessed changes in trajectory straightness and smoothness relative to the control target and differences between reach directions. We compared motor-network activity and connectivity using task-based and resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from participants with stroke and neurologically intact controls. To explore response variability, we tested associations between TMS response and motor impairment, resting-state connectivity, and the change in task-evoked activity at the stimulated region from planning to movement. Results: Suprathreshold PMd and PPC stimulation in both hemispheres improved trajectory straightness or smoothness during distal reaches relative to the control target. Suprathreshold contralesional PMd stimulation increased trajectory deviation and reduced smoothness during proximal reaches. Baseline performance during distal reaches was more closely related to motor impairment, and contralesional PMd effects were more favorable during distal than proximal reaches across all kinematic measures. Participants with stroke showed lower bilateral PMv activation during movement and stronger interhemispheric PPC connectivity. Only the change in task-evoked activity at the stimulated region from planning to movement was related to TMS response. Smaller changes relative to controls were associated with more favorable kinematic effects during distal reaches. Conclusions: Movements more affected after stroke were the most responsive to this type of stimulation. The response to TMS was also associated with task-evoked activity differences at the stimulated region between movement planning and execution. Neuromodulation may therefore be most effective when designed around both the pathophysiology of the cortical target and the type of movement.

item.title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

item.title: Task-evoked flexibility of intrinsic neural timescales is hierarchically organized, behaviorally relevant, and refined across two developmental stages
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cortical regions integrate temporal information over different timescales at rest, ranging from fast in sensorimotor regions to slow in the association cortex. Here, we study how far regions adapt these timescales to meet task demands, as well as how this \emph{timescale flexibility} is organized across the cortical hierarchy, and how it develops in humans. We quantified rest-to-task changes in intrinsic neural timescales, referred to as \emph{timescale deflections}, using fMRI data from four independent datasets totaling 1,712 participants aged 8--64 years. We found that timescales reduced under cognitive load in all four datasets, most strongly in association cortex, which partially flattened the resting-state timescale hierarchy. Individual differences in timescale deflections were organized along the sensorimotor-association (S-A) axis and tracked cognitive performance, both in adults and in youth. Next, in youth, deflections followed a two-stage developmental course: a generalized reduction throughout childhood, followed by a selective expansion in association cortex from mid-adolescence. Furthermore, the timing of these stages aligned with cortical gradients of inhibitory gene expression and intracortical myelin content, both features implicated in the opening and closing of critical periods of neural plasticity. Overall, our results demonstrate that task-evoked timescale flexibility is hierarchically organized, behaviorally and neurobiologically relevant, and refined across adolescence.

item.title: Development of Neonatal Functional Brain Network Organisation and Its Association with Childhood Neurodevelopmental Outcomes
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The human brain undergoes rapid dynamic changes in the neonatal period that are essential for later cognitive and behavioural performance. Using resting-state fMRI data from 394 neonates (325 term-born, 69 preterm-born) within the first month after birth, we characterised the early development of functional network organisation, the effects of preterm birth, and the association between neonatal functional organisation and later neurodevelopmental outcomes in infancy (18 months) and childhood (4-6 years). We found increased functional integration and segregation across a wide range of functional sub-networks and increased mean functional connectivity strength (mean FCS) within the subcortical and cerebellar regions with increasing PMA at scan. Compared with term-born neonates, preterm-born neonates showed significantly lower mean FCS, functional integration and segregation globally. We further showed that whilst neonatal functional brain network organisation was not associated with neurodevelopmental outcomes measured during infancy (18 months), it was associated with later neurodevelopmental outcomes in early childhood (4-6 years). Specifically, higher functional integration and segregation at birth were linked with lower SDQ total difficulties score at 4-6 years. Our findings suggest that neonatal functional brain organisation reflects not only transient developmental processes, but also stable individual differences that provide insight into neurodevelopmental outcomes in later childhood.

item.title: Faster peak alpha frequency precedes higher menstrual pain in adolescence
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Brain differences in chronic pain are almost always measured after years of pain experience, leaving unresolved whether they create vulnerability to pain or result from it. Uniquely, menstrual pain has a developmentally scheduled onset (menarche, the first menstrual period), allowing the brain to be characterized before and after pain exposure occurs. Here we used longitudinal 64-channel EEG to measure resting brain activity in adolescents once before (n=250) and twice after (n=161, n=140) menarche. Before their first period, adolescents who later reported higher menstrual pain (30 or greater on a 0 to 100 VAS) already showed faster occipital peak alpha frequency compared to those who reported lower menstrual pain, a difference that persisted in the early (3 to 14 months) post-menarche time period. In contrast, oscillatory power and functional connectivity did not differ by menstrual pain group, suggesting that the widespread functional brain alterations reported in adults with painful periods take years to emerge. Peak alpha frequency increased, and theta power and connectivity decreased across the menarchal transition, consistent with typical adolescent maturation. However, longitudinal analyses stratified by higher and lower menstrual pain group suggested group specific timings for these neurodevelopmental changes. Overall, these findings suggest that early menstrual pain is not associated with widespread alterations in neural oscillations, but aspects of menstrual pain susceptibility may be reflected in resting peak alpha frequency. To our knowledge, this is the first neurophysiological trait shown to precede the onset of menstrual pain.

item.title: Frequency-Specific Cognitive Control Network Hypoconnectivity in Adolescents With Elevated Externalizing Symptoms
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Externalizing symptoms during adolescence are associated with behavioral difficulties and an increased risk of adverse developmental outcomes, and are often accompanied by difficulties in self-regulation across cognitive and emotional domains. Although prior neuroimaging studies have reported altered brain connectivity in externalizing psychopathology, most evidence comes from functional magnetic resonance imaging, leaving frequency-specific electrophysiological network dynamics poorly understood. We examined resting-state electroencephalographic (EEG) functional connectivity in a community-based sample of 35 adolescents aged 13–15 years with relatively high or low parent-reported externalizing symptoms. Source-level connectivity was estimated using exact low-resolution electromagnetic tomography and lagged phase synchronization across delta-to-gamma frequency bands within the cognitive control network (CCN) and default mode network (DMN). Results Adolescents with higher externalizing symptoms showed reduced connectivity in five beta1- and gamma-band CCN connections, whereas no significant group differences were observed within the DMN. After adjustment for internalizing symptoms, bilateral anterior-insula connectivity in the beta1 band and left anterior insula–right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex connectivity in the gamma band remained significant. Lower left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex–right inferior frontal junction beta1 connectivity was also associated with greater self-reported physical aggression. Conclusions Elevated externalizing symptoms during adolescence may be linked to altered functional coordination within the cognitive control network. These findings highlight the potential value of frequency-resolved EEG connectivity for characterizing the neural correlates of adolescent externalizing symptoms.

item.title: Cross-Cohort Transportability of Multi-Family Resting-State EEG Microstate Dynamics in Parkinson's Disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Resting-state electroencephalography (EEG) microstates provide a millisecond-scale representation of large-scale brain-state dynamics, but the cross-cohort stability of Parkinson's disease (PD)-related microstate signatures remains uncertain. We tested whether a multi-family representation of canonical A/B/C/D microstate sequences---integrating static descriptors, directed transitions, flow-related measures, and sequence complexity---retains disease-related information across increasingly stringent validation levels. The development analysis used repeated stratified cross-validation, followed by leakage-aware fold-wise template estimation and locked external testing on an independent OpenNeuro cohort. Random forest achieved a development-cohort ROC-AUC of 0.823, whereas performance fell to near chance during external testing (ROC-AUC = 0.513). In the same feature space, a dataset-origin classifier achieved ROC-AUC = 0.966, demonstrating substantial cross-cohort distribution shift. These findings show that resting-state microstate dynamics contain PD-related information within a cohort, but that the present representation is not sufficiently stable across cohorts. Cross-cohort validation and explicit assessment of dataset shift are therefore essential when evaluating EEG microstate features as reproducible electrophysiological markers.

item.title: A Dual-Stream Spatio-Temporal Network with Bidirectional Rectification for Differential Diagnosis of Dementia using EEG
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Accurate differential diagnosis between Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) is of critical importance for the early screening of neurodegenerative diseases. Scalp electroencephalogram (EEG), as a non-invasive neurophysiological detection tool with excellent temporal resolution, has been widely adopted in dementia screening research. However, the inherent low signal-to-noise ratio and non-stationarity of scalp EEG signals, combined with the highly overlapping pathological rhythms between AD and FTD patients, render existing single-domain representation methods incapable of achieving precise pathological differentiation. To address this challenge, this paper proposes a dual-stream spatio-temporal network. In this framework, multiscale temporal features and effective connectivity graph features are extracted in parallel, followed by their integration. However, directly fusing the features from the two streams tends to amplify their respective noises. Therefore, the Spatio-Temporal Feature Fusion Based on Bidirectional Rectification module is proposed to execute dynamic noise suppression on the features and subsequently performs deep feature fusion via a cross-attention mechanism. Furthermore, this paper applies knowledge distillation using attention maps to address the issue of imbalanced sample distributions in the dataset. Experimental results on the ADFTD-RS dataset show that the proposed framework yields a subject-level accuracy of 60.00\% and an F1-score of 57.44\%, showing measurable improvements over several baseline methods. This work offers a feasible approach for the computer-aided differential diagnosis of dementia based on resting-state EEG.

item.title: Infra-slow brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions reveal a co-ordinated multisystem physiological network in humans.
item.description:
The Journal of physiology
Growing evidence indicates that brain continuously interacts with other physiological systems through neural and non-neural pathways. The brain-heart and brain-gut axes play a central role in homoeostasis, allostasis and behaviour, but also in cognitive aspects, including emotion and decision-making. Disruptions in these axes have been linked to a wide range of cardiovascular, neurological and psychiatric disorders. Despite this evidence, triadic crosstalk between the brain, heart and gut remains largely unexplored. Brain activity, cardiac autonomic fluctuations and gastric rhythms all exhibit slow temporal components in resting state, suggesting that brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions may occur over time scales from the infra-slow (0.01-0.1 Hz) physiological range. Using open-access electrophysiological recordings from 28 healthy subjects at rest, we extracted time-varying power dynamics describing the activity of the three organs: brain alpha power, cardiac sympathetic and parasympathetic indices, and the power of the gastric rhythm. Statistical associations among these organs were quantified using the maximal information coefficient across the extended temporal delay range. Physiological interactions were confirmed using surrogate-based testing, which allowed us to construct the network topology of interactions between the three organs. Our findings show that triadic brain-heart-gut interactions form a multidirectional network primarily at infra-slow time scales during resting state. This study offers one of the first insights into the physiology of brain-heart-gut interplay, providing a methodological baseline for the development of more comprehensive biomarkers based on network dynamics capable of linking pathological conditions to dysregulation across multiple organ systems. KEY POINTS: First in-human, non-invasive investigation of parallel brain-heart-gut electrophysiological interactions in awake, healthy subjects. We analysed simultaneous electroencephalographic (EEG), electrocardiographic (ECG) and electrogastrographic (EGG) recordings and quantified strength and temporal scale of the derived time series associations to construct a large-scale network of interactions. We found that brain-heart-gut interactions extend into the infra-slow range (0.01-0.1 Hz), indicating that spontaneous fluctuations in the electrophysiological activity of one organ at rest are typically followed by corresponding changes in the other two. We consistently found a robust brain-heart-gut network topology across subjects, with multidirectional interactions and bodily dynamics converging towards midline central-posterior EEG regions. These findings provide one of the first endeavours in characterizing the physiology of brain-heart-gut interactions and a methodology with strong biomarker development potential.

item.title: Gamma-band network segregation links corollary discharge dysfunction and anomalous self-experiences in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Schizophrenia research
Anomalous self-experiences (ASEs) are a core feature of psychotic disorders and reflect disturbances in ipseity. Impairments in corollary discharge mechanism have been proposed as a neurobiological substrate of ASEs, and an imbalance between brain network integration and segregation, may impair the coherent flow of mental contents, thereby disrupting their fluid and implicit character. However, the relationship between corollary discharge and functional network properties has not been directly examined. This link was assessed in thirty participants with schizophrenia and thirty healthy controls. Functional network was computed using the Phase Locking Value (PLV) from resting-state EEG in the gamma band and two parameters were calculated: the clustering coefficient (ClC, as a proxy for segregation) and the path length (PL, as a proxy for integration); corollary discharge was indexed by N1 suppression in a talk-listen paradigm; and ASEs were evaluated using the 'Inventory of Psychotic-Like Anomalous Self-Experiences' (IPASE) total score. Patients with schizophrenia showed significantly greater gamma-band network segregation and lower integration than healthy controls. Moreover, higher segregation in this band was associated with reduced N1 suppression and greater ASEs severity in patients, whereas network integration was not associated with N1 suppression nor ASEs. These findings suggest that excessive gamma-band network segregation may be correlated with disrupted corollary discharge functioning and may compromise the distinction between self-generated and external stimuli. Therefore, it may alter the sense of ipseity by interfering with the integration of mental contents into the flow of consciousness, thereby contributing to greater severity of ASEs.

item.title: Reduced short-lag autoregressive carry-over in resting-state latent dynamics in major depressive disorder.
item.description:
Psychiatry research. Neuroimaging
Major depressive disorder (MDD) is increasingly characterized as a disorder of brain dynamics, but the temporal scale on which resting-state activity differs from healthy controls remains unclear. We analyzed resting-state fMRI data from 71 participants (51 MDD, 20 controls; OpenNeuro ds002748) using bilateral grid-extracted left-right difference signals projected into a control-defined latent space. Across 30 analysis configurations spanning five denoising pipelines, three latent dimensionalities, and two left-right correction settings, MDD showed reduced mean lag-1 autocorrelation in 24 of 30 configurations (integrated β = -0.0321, p = 0.036) and reduced AR(1) gain φ in 24 of 30 (β = -0.0316, p = 0.037), both robust to adjustment for pipeline, age, sex, and head motion. The broader autocorrelation area under lags 1-10 was not significantly reduced (β = -0.0099, p = 0.22), and lag-by-lag analysis localized the group difference specifically to lag 1. A model-comparison analysis identified AR-gain reduction as one of three competing candidate generative transformations rather than the unique winner. MDD is thus associated with a focal short-lag autoregressive carry-over reduction, a candidate latent-dynamical phenotype rather than a fully identified mechanism.

item.title: Altered white matter functional activity and connectivity in pretreatment breast cancer: exploratory associations with affective symptoms.
item.description:
Brain research bulletin
Objective Resting-state fMRI studies in breast cancer have predominantly focused on gray matter, with limited attention to white matter functional organization. This study investigated white matter functional activity and connectivity before treatment and their associations with anxiety and depressive symptoms. Methods Female patients with breast cancer (BC) were recruited from Zhejiang Provincial Tongde Hospital from November 2023 to December 2025. Amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (ALFF) and fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuation (fALFF) were used to compare local white matter functional activity between the BC and healthy control (HC) groups. Seed-based functional connectivity (FC) analysis was then performed to investigate whole-brain white matter FC alterations. Correlations between clinical scale scores and rs-fMRI indices were analyzed. Results Compared with HCs, patients with BC showed altered ALFF/fALFF in the anterior and posterior corona radiata, internal capsule, posterior thalamic radiation, body of the corpus callosum, pontine crossing tract, left superior cerebellar peduncle, and left superior longitudinal fasciculus. Seed-based analysis revealed decreased FC within the bilateral anterior corona radiata and between the body of the corpus callosum and right anterior corona radiata, and increased FC between the left superior cerebellar peduncle and left posterior thalamic radiation. Higher ALFF in the body of the corpus callosum and reduced FC between this region and the right anterior corona radiata were associated with higher Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale scores at an uncorrected threshold. Neither association survived FDR correction. Conclusion Patients with BC showed altered white matter functional activity and connectivity before cancer-related treatment, suggesting that pretreatment brain functional alterations may also involve white matter functional organization. The relationship between these white matter changes and anxiety or depressive symptoms remains exploratory.

item.title: Left Temporoparietal Neural Synchrony Tracks Cooperative Performance Across Adult Dyads
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Cooperation requires interacting individuals to coordinate their actions toward shared goals, and interpersonal neural synchrony (INS) has been proposed as a neural correlate of this coordination. However, the relationship between INS and cooperative performance remains heterogeneous, and relatively little is known about how it varies across social relationships. The present study examined INS and behavioral performance during a naturalistic cooperative tabletop Jenga task in close-friend, romantic-partner, and mother--child dyads (N = 284 participants). Brain activity was simultaneously recorded using functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) hyperscanning, and INS was quantified using wavelet transform coherence across the bilateral inferior frontal gyrus (IFG) and temporoparietal junction (TPJ). Cooperative performance was assessed using tower collapse and the number of valid turns completed during the game. True interacting dyads exhibited significantly greater neural synchrony than surrogate dyads across all examined regional pairings (d range = 0.35-0.55), indicating robust interaction-related inter-brain synchrony. Behavioral performance was not associated with INS at the whole-network level. Region-specific analyses, however, showed that tower collapse was associated with reduced synchrony in the left TPJ-left TPJ (p Bonf = 0.009) and left TPJ-right TPJ (p Bonf = 0.017) pairings, whereas the number of valid turns was unrelated to INS. Follow-up analyses further indicated that the association between tower collapse and left TPJ--left TPJ synchrony was present in close-friend (p Bonf = 0.020) and romantic-partner (p Bonf = 0.026) dyads but not in mother-child dyads. These findings suggest that the behavioral relevance of interpersonal neural synchrony is not uniform, but depends on the neural systems involved, the specific index of cooperative performance, and the relational and developmental context in which interaction unfolds.

item.title: Accentuated Divergence, Constrained Expression: Autistic Traits Modulate the Creative Brain in Adults with ADHD
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Background Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition, and co-occurring autistic traits may shape its phenotypic expression. Although creativity has been discussed as a relative strength in ADHD, it remains unclear whether autistic traits are associated with different dimensions of creativity in adults with ADHD and whether large-scale brain networks contribute to these associations. Methods We compared divergent thinking (DT) and real-life creativity between 65 adults with ADHD and 73 neurotypical controls. We used subgroup comparisons, partial correlation analyses, and multiple regression models to determine the effects of autistic traits (ATs) on creativity dimensions within the ADHD cohort. Guided by prior creativity-network research, we analyzed resting-state functional connectivity (FC) of the Default Mode Network (DMN) and Frontoparietal Network (FPN) to uncover the neural mechanisms. Results The ADHD cohort demonstrated significantly higher scores on both DT ( p s = 0.002–0.009) and real-life creativity measures ( p s = 0.011–0.017) compared to the neurotypical control group. Importantly, increased ATs within the ADHD group were associated with a dissociated creativity profile, showing positive associations with DT but negative associations with real-life creativity. At the neural level, stronger right DMN–FPN connectivity mediated positive associations between ATs and DT performance (ps = 0.007–0.018), but mediated a negative association between ATs and self-reported imagination (p = 0.029). Conclusions In individuals with ADHD, co-occurring ATs exert a paradoxical effect on creativity, enhancing DT while compromising real-life creative achievement. In this subgroup with ADHD and elevated ATs, interventions should capitalize on ATs-associated ideational strengths while circumventing translational barriers, to enhance real-world creative outcomes.

item.title: Dose-dependent myelin g-ratio alterations in the white matter of 16p11.2 copy number variations
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Copy number variations (CNVs) at the 16p11.2 locus are major genetic risk factors for neurodevelopmental conditions and drive reciprocal alterations in cerebral white matter structure and connectivity. However, whether these alterations reflect differences in the axonal or myelin compartments remains unresolved with conventional diffusion MRI. We combined diffusion MRI with magnetization transfer saturation mapping across two ComBat-harmonized cohorts comprising 80 controls, 26 16p11.2 deletion carriers, and 13 duplication carriers. We quantified axonal volume, myelin volume, and aggregate g-ratio of white matter tracts forming the structural connectome. Metrics were evaluated using normative modeling across tract length, resting-state functional networks, and cortical nodes. We additionally examined 29 individuals carrying other neurodevelopmental CNVs. 16p11.2 gene dosage was associated with regional reciprocal differences in tract axonal volume, with greater volume in deletion carriers and lower volume in duplication carriers. In contrast, myelin volume did not differ significantly from controls. This mismatch resulted in pervasive aggregate g-ratio alterations, with higher g-ratios (relatively thinner myelin sheaths) in deletion carriers and lower g-ratios (relatively thicker sheaths) in duplication carriers. Regional g-ratio alterations also extended to other neurodevelopmental CNVs. These findings resolve some of the biological ambiguity underlying white matter alterations in 16p11.2 CNV carriers, implicating the axonal compartment while revealing comparatively stable myelin volume. The disrupted axon-myelin scaling results in connectome-wide g-ratio alterations and may represent a shared microstructural hallmark of genetic neurodevelopmental risk.

item.title: Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Science advances
Schizophrenia disrupts both how people perceive the world and how they express and act on their thoughts, yet these symptoms are usually studied separately. Using magnetoencephalography during multisensory and motor tasks, we tested whether reduced event-related beta-band (15 to 30 hertz) modulation, a signal implicated in predictive control, provides a candidate neural marker across these domains. Compared to healthy individuals, patients showed diminished beta changes during sensory processing and movement completion, suggesting reduced flexibility in updating internal models. This neural pattern covaried with audiovisual simultaneity-judgment behavior, disorganized natural speech, and greater clinical severity. These findings suggest that distributed beta modulation may serve as a candidate cross-domain marker associated with perceptual, motor, and language disturbances in schizophrenia, motivating future studies that directly test predictive updating mechanisms.

item.title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners' spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest within-network coherence, marking them as the central hub of the system, and distinguishing them from less central and less coherent domain-general regions. Together, the findings reveal how the brain dynamically decomposes complex spatial instruction, preserving parietal-centered spatial processing, while coordinating support from premotor, domain-general, and language systems. These findings begin to reveal how spatial cognition operates within the complexity of formal instruction.

item.title: Thalamocortical dysconnectivity shapes cortical hierarchy disruption across illness durations in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Schizophrenia is increasingly conceptualized as a disorder of circuit-level dysfunction. However, how thalamocortical abnormalities differ across cohorts with varying illness durations and relate to large-scale cortical hierarchical organization remains unclear. Methods We analyzed resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 1,223 patients with schizophrenia and 1,224 matched healthy controls across 12 datasets. The datasets were grouped as early-, middle-, and late-stage cohorts. Connectivity gradient mapping was applied to characterize thalamocortical organization, and computational modeling evaluated simulated hierarchical changes after modifying thalamic-salience connectivity. Results We identified a schizophrenia-relevant sensorimotor-salience-association axis that captures systematic differences in thalamocortical abnormality profiles across the stage cohorts. Along this axis, case-control effects in association regions were positive in the early-stage cohort but negative in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, whereas sensorimotor regions showed the converse pattern. This cross-cohort pattern was accompanied by reduced cortical hierarchical separation in cohorts with longer illness duration. In contrast, salience-related thalamic regions showed negative case-control effects in all three stage cohorts, with larger effect sizes in the middle- and late-stage cohorts, and these alterations were associated with clinical symptoms. Computational modification of thalamic-salience connectivity increased simulated cortical hierarchical differentiation, particularly in the middle-stage cohort. Conclusions These findings indicate that thalamocortical dysconnectivity, centered on disrupted thalamic-salience interactions, is associated with systematic differences in cortical hierarchical organization across cohorts. The cross-cohort pattern of salience-related abnormalities highlights thalamic-salience coupling as a circuit-level link to cortical hierarchical differentiation and a candidate for future mechanistic and interventional investigation.

item.title: Driving Simulation Methods for Assessing Post-Injury Driving Performance After Mild Traumatic Brain Injury: A Scoping Review.
item.description:
Accident; analysis and prevention
Driving is a cognitively demanding task that involves the continuous integration of attention, executive control, visual processing, and motor coordination. Mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI) may disrupt these functions and affect driving performance during recovery. Driving simulation is increasingly used to examine post-mTBI driving performance, yet substantial heterogeneity exists in simulator platforms, task designs, and outcome selection. This scoping review characterized driving simulation methodologies used to assess post-mTBI driving performance and examined patterns of mTBI-related findings across reported outcomes. A systematic search of seven electronic databases identified 12 eligible publications between 2017 and 2026. Publications were synthesized by participant characteristics, time since injury, simulator platform, task demands, and outcomes. Across publications, mTBI-related findings were most frequently reported for vehicle control metrics, particularly lane position variability and speed regulation. mTBI-related differences were most often condition-specific, including differences during curves, hazard events, and manipulated cognitive load or dual-task conditions. Cognitive measures also demonstrated mTBI-related differences and associations to driving performance, particularly those assessing executive functioning and processing speed domains. Differences were observed across all post-injury intervals, including ≥ 15 days, with a small number of related publications reporting performance differences after symptom resolution. However, the predominantly cross-sectional evidence does not establish whether these differences persist over time within the same individuals. Findings suggest that driving simulation can provide a useful controlled method for examining functional driving performance following mTBI across varying road environments and task demands. Future work should prioritize standardizing simulator outcomes and validating simulator performance against on-road, naturalistic-driving, and crash-related outcomes.

item.title: Multimodal Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Relapse in Major Depressive Disorder.
item.description:
JAMA psychiatry
Importance Early identification of patients at high risk of relapse is key to personalized preventive strategies in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, current predictive models do not adequately account for the multimodal factors contributing to MDD relapse and fail to provide clinically meaningful predictions. Objective To predict relapse within 2 years in patients with MDD by using a comprehensive machine learning pipeline that integrates an unprecedented set of multimodal data.
