Design, setting, and participants This naturalistic longitudinal prognostic study used data from the Marburg-Münster Affective Disorders Cohort Study, with baseline assessments collected from October 2014 to May 2019 and follow-up approximately 2 years later, between October 2016 and June 2021. Data analysis was conducted between July 2024 and June 2026. The study was performed at 2 sites in Germany (Marburg and Münster), with participants recruited from psychiatric inpatient and outpatient departments and the general population. Patients meeting diagnostic criteria for current or lifetime MDD without history of neurological or severe somatic conditions were included. Exposure Natural course of illness in patients with MDD. Main outcomes and measures Balanced accuracy (BACC) for binary prediction of relapse vs no relapse during 2-year follow-up served as the primary outcome. Baseline features comprised 9 modalities including clinical and psychometric data, 4 structural and functional magnetic resonance imaging modalities, genetics, neurocognition, blood markers, and gut microbiome. Results A total of 564 patients with a current or lifetime MDD diagnosis were included (367 female [65.1%]; mean [SD] age, 37.34 [13.38] years). A total of 270 patients relapsed during the 2-year follow-up, while 294 did not. Mean (SD) BACC for the prediction of relapse ranged from 47.21% (5.85%) to 64.43% (6.63%). The best-performing model was solely based on few clinical relapse risk factors, while multimodal data integration did not improve performance. Conclusions and relevance In this prognostic study, the models achieved moderate accuracy, yet the results suggest limited scope for guiding individual-level clinical decision-making. Predictive performance was largely driven by established clinical risk factors, indicating limited incremental value of multimodal measures when assessed at a single time point. Future advances may instead benefit from dynamic modeling approaches that more closely align temporally evolving multimodal markers with longitudinal clinical outcomes.

item.title: Infantile amnesia results from differential memory retrieval in humans
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Infantile amnesia, the inability to recall memories from our earliest years, is the most common form of forgetting in mammals 1 . Whether early memories never form, decay, or persist but become inaccessible remains unknown. Here, we investigated the nature of forgetting during the infantile amnesia period by longitudinally testing toddlers aged 18-24 months across the complete memory cycle from encoding, initial retrieval one day later, and delayed retrieval up to six months later, in a novel naturalistic episodic memory paradigm. Computational modelling revealed that forgetting during the infantile amnesia period was heterogeneous. Toddlers were as likely to retain the full memory as to lose it completely, while nearly a quarter retained only part of the memory. Encoding accuracy predicted which toddlers retained the full memory at the test one day later, but not at the delayed test up to six months on. Instead, a retrieval-specific EEG signature predicted complete, but not partial, memory retrieval, distinguishing which toddlers had retained the full memory before their behavioural response. Finally, leveraging the COVID-19 pandemic as a natural experiment, we found that maternal immune activation during pregnancy, as in rodents 2 , alters vulnerability to infantile forgetting in humans. Together, these findings show that early memories formed during the infantile amnesia period are not simply erased but persist in an increasingly inaccessible form, a transformation whose trajectory can be shaped by both the neural retrieval mechanism and the prenatal environment.

item.title: Intelligent systems distribute memory across internal and embodied resources
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Intelligent systems do not operate in isolation from the body, yet how bodily actions support internal computation remains unclear. Here we show that primates and artificial agents recruit eye movements to maintain beliefs about hidden goals when internal computation is constrained. In a naturalistic navigation task, both systems spontaneously tracked goals with their eyes after they disappeared from view. This strategy emerged in artificial agents only when internal memory was constrained, identifying resource constraints as a driver of memory externalization. Restricting gaze impaired performance in both systems, while natural behavioral variability and causal perturbations in agents established a direct influence of oculomotor state on internal beliefs about hidden goals. Across agents, varying the reliability of internal memory and gaze redistributed goal information between internal and embodied states. The same resource-allocation principle predicted the distribution of goal information in macaque parietal cortex, where greater reliance on gaze was accompanied by weaker gaze-independent neural representations. Together, these findings identify eye movements as embodied memory and reveal a convergent principle across intelligent systems: memory is allocated across internal and embodied resources according to their reliability.

item.title: Neurodegeneration epicenters: Distinct network mechanisms of dopaminergic treatment in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
Neural regeneration research
Abstract Parkinson's disease exhibits heterogeneous spatiotemporal patterns of neurodegeneration. Dopaminergic therapy improves motor symptoms by modulating brain function in affected regions, yet whether the neural mechanisms through which dopaminergic therapy exerts its effects are linked to this heterogeneity of neurodegeneration remains unclear. A connectivity-based epicenter framework combined with spectral dynamic causal modeling was applied to resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 160 drug-naïve Parkinson's disease patients and 174 healthy controls to identify subtype-specific degenerative epicenters and characterize directional interactions among affected regions. Ninety-seven patients additionally underwent an acute levodopa challenge to evaluate how dopaminergic modulation influences these interactions and relates to symptom improvements. Two distinct Parkinson's disease subtypes were identified: subtype 1 was characterized by degenerative epicenters predominantly located in subcortical and cerebellar regions, whereas subtype 2 exhibited epicenters primarily involving cortical regions. Both subtypes exhibited widespread dysregulation of directional interactions among epicenter regions relative to healthy controls. Levodopa treatment partially reversed these network abnormalities in a manner specific to each subtype, notably within cerebellar vermis in subtype 1 and frontal cortex in subtype 2. Symptom improvements were linked to distinct network interactions: in subtype 1, tremor correlated with the thalamus, midbrain nuclei, and cerebellar vermis, whereas bradykinesia primarily involved the cerebellar vermis; in subtype 2, rigidity improvements mapped to frontal cortex and limbic regions, and bradykinesia to limbic regions. These findings suggest that Parkinson's disease involves distinct epicenter networks in each subtype, with widespread directional dysregulation contributing to symptom diversity in patients. Levodopa treatment selectively modulates these network interactions, shedding light on the mechanisms underlying treatment heterogeneity and guiding precision-targeted therapeutic strategies.

item.title: Functional neuroimaging as a tool to understand social determinants of health in cognitive aging and ADRD: a scoping review
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The social, structural, and physical conditions in which individuals live, work, and age, collectively termed social determinants of health (SDOH), are associated with risk of Alzheimer's disease and related dementias (ADRD). Differences in brain function in later life may offer understanding of how SDOH become biologically embedded and confer differential ADRD risk. However, how functional neuroimaging techniques have been used to study SDOH in cognitive aging and ADRD has yet to be systematically characterized. We therefore conducted a scoping review. Three databases were searched, 2,930 articles were screened, and 41 studies were included. Education was the most frequently studied SDOH domain, accounting for 65.9% (k = 27) of studies, followed by economic and occupation (k = 9, 22.0%), social and community (k = 5, 12.2%), food (k = 4, 9.8%), and physical environment (k = 3, 7.3%). Of the 41 studies, five (12.2%) examined multidomain determinants and one study (2.4%) examined three determinants each from different domains. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was most frequently employed (k = 31, 75.6%), followed by electroencephalography (EEG; k = 7, 17.1%), and magnetoencephalography (MEG; k = 4, 9.8%). One study (2.4%) employed a multimodal approach, while none used functional near-infrared spectroscopy. Resting state paradigms (k = 27, 65.9%) outnumbered task-based (k = 14, 34.1%) and most studies were cross-sectional (k = 38, 92.7%). The predominant focus on education, fMRI, and cross-sectional designs highlights many opportunities for future investigation of how SDOH may be associated with later life brain function.

item.title: Problematic social media and gaming use, screen time, and youth mental health and brain structure in the ABCD Study
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
In an increasingly digital age, knowing which kinds of screen use relate to mental health in adolescents could help guide prevention efforts for a vulnerable population. Earlier work has examined this question, but the findings have been difficult to interpret. For instance, most studies measure screen use in hours, while it may be more informative to know whether adolescents have difficulty controlling their use. This is especially important now that adolescents use screens for school, games and contact with friends. Whether these patterns are reflected in the brain also remains largely unexplored. ABCD Study release 7.0 (N=11,860) is well suited to these questions because of its comprehensive profiling across neuroimaging, behavioral and clinical domains. In a preregistered study, we examined how screen time, problematic social media use (SMAQ) and problematic video game use (VGAQ) relate to parent-rated mental health, brain structure and resting-state connectivity. All five confirmatory associations were positive but small (β = 0.051 to 0.173) and remained consistent across several robustness checks. In the same participants, the problematic use scales were more strongly related to attention problems than hours of use were. The association between screen time and anxiety problems was present in male but not female participants. More screen time was associated with slightly smaller putamen and caudate volumes, while resting-state connectivity did not predict SMAQ. In exploratory analyses, SMAQ predicted later attention problems more than the reverse, while for gaming, attention problems predicted later VGAQ more strongly. Most of the association seemed to come from problematic use rather than use time by itself. Overall, the effects were small but consistent, in line with earlier work in the ABCD Study. We hope this analysis can contribute to a better understanding of how social media and gaming relate to adolescent mental health and brain development.

item.title: Personalized Network Mapping Reveals State-Trait Dissociation of Frontoparietal Connectivity in Adolescent Depression: A Longitudinal Study
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Prior research linking resting-state networks (RSNs) to adolescent depression has yielded inconsistent findings, partly because group-average templates poorly capture individual brains; a mismatch that may be especially consequential during adolescence, when RSNs grow increasingly heterogeneous across individuals. Using a personalized analysis pipeline in the longitudinal Characterizing Adolescent Trajectories of Depression cohort (38 depressed adolescents [28 female]; ages 14–18; 181 usable scans; avg. participation: 446.18 days), we derived individualized definitions of three canonical depression-related RSNs. Because longitudinal RSN connectivity may reflect both trait-like vulnerability and state-like symptom fluctuation, we used mixed-effects models to decompose connectivity profiles into both components. FPN connectivity showed a significant state-trait dissociation: chronically elevated connectivity predicted greater average symptom burden, while transient increases predicted momentary relief. These effects were undetectable using group-atlas estimates. We suggest FPN connectivity plays a dual, compensatory role in adolescent depression and demonstrate that personalized definitions can reveal clinically meaningful brain–symptom associations.

item.title: Predictive EEG Signatures of Alzheimer's Disease: A Cross-Validated, Cross-Method Analysis Using ANCOVA Filtering and Sparse Logistic Regression
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) changes how the brain’s electrical activity behaves, and these changes can, in principle, be picked up directly from a resting-state EEG recording without any invasive testing. This study asks a much narrower question: does a small subset of four EEG-derived measurement families, namely signal complexity, spectral power, functional connectivity and network topology, reliably separate individuals with AD from Healthy Controls (HC), and does that separation hold up under strict, leakage-free testing? Using a public dataset of 36 AD and 29 HC subjects, candidate features were selected through permutation-based ANCOVA with false discovery rate correction, controlling for age and gender, and each selected feature was then re-checked using a complementary method (Mann-Whitney U with FDR correction, plus network-based statistics for connectivity), applied to the same subjects, to confirm the finding wasn’t an artifact of the first method’s particular assumptions. Agreement between the two methods was strong for signal complexity (Jaccard = 0.85) and spectral power (Jaccard = 0.87), essentially perfect for two of the four network measures (Jaccard = 1.00), and weaker for connectivity (Jaccard = 0.60, assessed at the level of frequency bands). A sparse logistic regression classifier was then trained using 5-fold cross-validation in which feature selection was independently repeated inside each fold, a design specifically intended to stop information from test subjects leaking into which features get chosen. This classifier reached 78.5% ± 5.8% accuracy at discriminating AD from HC (sensitivity 0.803 ± 0.116, specificity 0.753 ± 0.100, AUC 0.808 ± 0.134). A single spectral power feature was among the two features retained in three of the five folds, more than any other individual feature. Taken together, the results point to a real but modest EEG signature of AD in this dataset, identified using a validation design built specifically so that reported accuracy reflects genuine generalization rather than an artifact of how the features were selected.

item.title: Molecularly distinct neurodegeneration shapes the DOPA-dependent dynamic of large-scale brain connectomics in GBA-associated Parkinson’s disease
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract GBA1-associated Parkinson’s disease (GBA1-PD) is a biologically distinct synucleinopathy associated with glucocerebrosidase deficiency, lysosomal dysfunction, and more extensive cortical neurodegeneration. How these molecular abnormalities shape large-scale cortical network dynamics in vivo remains incompletely understood. This study aimed to characterize resting-state EEG functional connectivity and network topology in GBA1-PD and to determine whether GBA1-related molecular pathology is associated with a distinct oscillatory connectome signature and its modulation by dopaminergic treatment. We recorded resting-state EEG in 22 patients with PD (GBA1-PD = 7; LRRK2-PD = 5; sporadic PD = 10) together with 14 age-matched healthy controls. EEG was acquired in OFF and ON dopaminergic states. Functional connectivity was estimated using imaginary coherence (ImCoh) and phase-locking value (PLV) across canonical frequency bands, while network organization was quantified using the graph-theoretical clustering coefficient. Linear mixed-effects models were used to assess therapy- and subtype-specific effects. GBA1-PD exhibited a selective increase in gamma-band clustering coefficient in the ON condition (p = 0.044), which was not observed in LRRK2 or sporadic PD. PLV-based analyses highlighted opposite clustering changes in GBA1 and LRRK2 patients. ImCoh analyses further revealed different therapy-related connectivity changes in genetic and sporadic PD across all frequency bands (all p ≤ 0.0035). Compared with healthy controls, PD was associated with widespread disruption of cortico-cortical connectivity. All significant effects were abolished in surrogate-data analyses, supporting their physiological specificity. Resting-state EEG connectomics may reveal genotype-specific network alterations in GBA1-PD and their modulation by dopaminergic treatment, supporting a relationship between genetic background and large-scale brain network dynamics.

item.title: Termination Failure as a Framework for Bipolar Disorder: Candidate Mechanisms and Testable Pharmacological Predictions
item.description:
[预印本] Preprints.org
Bioenergetic accounts of bipolar disorder (BD) have been shaped by a persistent observation: resting brain ATP and phosphocreatine often appear near-normal, even in symptomatic patients. Challenge-based work has moved the field beyond static measures, showing that patients fail to sustain ATP under high demand, and has framed the core abnormality as a deficit of capacity. This review re-examines that literature from a control perspective and argues that the capacity to terminate demand-driven energetic upregulation has been largely untested, chiefly because resting and single-challenge designs cannot resolve return kinetics. The argument is developed in three steps. First, we review how neuronal energy supply is matched to demand, giving comparable weight to adenine-nucleotide feedback, mitochondrial calcium signalling, and phosphotransfer buffering, and we note evidence that cytosolic ATP and ATP:ADP are strikingly stable during physiological activity. Second, we set out three candidate implementations of the termination step — mitochondrial Ca² efflux via NCLX, adenine ⁺ nucleotide feedback, and the creatine kinase–phosphocreatine system — and grade the evidence for each, distinguishing findings obtained in BD from those extrapolated from other systems. None has been assayed directly in BD tissue. Third, using a minimal control-loop model, we show that reduced termination capacity alone does not generate cycling; depending on parameters it produces slowed return, latching, persistent elevation, or sustained oscillation. Cycling therefore requires additional conditions, which we state explicitly. We close with pharmacological strategies that would discriminate among the candidates.

item.title: The network localization and underlying biological basis of heterogeneous structural and functional brain abnormalities in insomnia disorder.
item.description:
Sleep
Insomnia disorder (ID) has become a prevalent sleep disorder worldwide, yet its underlying neural mechanisms remain unclear due to heterogeneous neuroimaging findings and uncertain network localization. We identified brain structural and functional abnormality locations associated with ID from 63 published neuroimaging studies, including 3391 patients and 3433 healthy controls. Using coordinate network mapping combined with a normative connectome database, we mapped these abnormalities to large-scale brain networks of ID across imaging modalities and further decoded them by integrating microscale chemo-architectural, cellular, and cognitive maps. The structural network widely involved the ventral attention (VAN), sensorimotor (SMN), dorsal attention (DAN) and default mode network (DMN); the task-induced network showed a similar but less extensive pattern, predominantly implicating the VAN, DMN, SMN and subcortical network (SCN); in contrast, the resting-state network was largely confined to the left middle frontal gyrus and the bilateral mid-cingulate cortex. Molecular mapping revealed both shared and distinct neurotransmitter signatures across the three networks, involving cholinergic, histaminergic, glutamatergic, noradrenergic, and opioid systems. Cellular decoding showed relatively selective associations of the structural and task-based networks with glial cells and excitatory neurons, whereas the resting-state network exhibited broader associations with glial cells and multiple excitatory and inhibitory neuronal subtypes. Cognitive decoding linked structural and task-based networks to sensorimotor processing and the resting-state network to memory-related functions. Our findings reconcile heterogeneous neuroimaging results and reveal neurobiological substrates of ID from a network perspective, providing a promising biomarker and paving the way for circuit-based precision therapies of ID.
